compare-amanitas.summary: The Amanita family side by side: warts, rings, volvas and flesh colour. Never eat any Amanita.

nettle.name: Common nettle
nettle.season: Young tops Mar–Jun (and regrowth after cutting); seeds Aug–Oct; fibre stems Aug–Oct
nettle.habitat: Almost everywhere with rich soil: hedgerows, woodland edges, riverbanks, around farms, ruins and old campsites
nettle.summary: Stinging herb with toothed, heart-shaped leaves in opposite pairs. A top wild green when cooked and the best UK fibre for cordage.

white-dead-nettle.name: White dead-nettle
white-dead-nettle.habitat: Hedge banks, verges, waste ground, field edges, often growing among stinging nettles
white-dead-nettle.summary: Nettle-like plant with no sting and white, hooded two-lipped flowers in whorls. Young leaves and flowers are edible.

dandelion.name: Dandelion
dandelion.season: Leaves all year (best Feb–Apr before flowering); flowers Mar–Oct (peak Apr–May); roots Sep–Mar
dandelion.habitat: Lawns, verges, pasture, waste ground: almost everywhere
dandelion.summary: Rosette of jagged leaves with a single yellow flower on a hollow, milky stalk. Every part is edible.

wild-garlic.name: Wild garlic
wild-garlic.season: Leaves Feb–May; flowers Apr–Jun; seed pods May–Jun
wild-garlic.habitat: Damp, shady broadleaf woodland, stream banks and hedges, often as dense carpets, especially on chalk and limestone
wild-garlic.summary: Carpets of broad, soft leaves smelling strongly of garlic, with white star-shaped flowers. Deadly lookalikes grow in the same woods.

three-cornered-leek.name: Three-cornered leek
three-cornered-leek.habitat: Hedge banks, verges and waste ground, especially in the south-west and near the coast
three-cornered-leek.summary: Garlic-scented plant with a sharply triangular stem and drooping white bell flowers with a green stripe.

garlic-mustard.name: Garlic mustard
garlic-mustard.season: Leaves Feb–Jun (second-year plants), new rosettes autumn; flowers Apr–Jun
garlic-mustard.habitat: Hedgerows, woodland edges, shady verges and walls
garlic-mustard.summary: Upright hedgerow plant with heart-shaped, toothed leaves that smell of garlic when crushed and small white four-petalled flowers.

cleavers.name: Cleavers
cleavers.habitat: Hedgerows, field edges, gardens, scrambling over other plants
cleavers.summary: Straggling plant whose stems, leaves and seeds are covered in tiny hooks, so it sticks to clothes. Young tips are edible cooked.

ribwort-plantain.name: Ribwort plantain
ribwort-plantain.habitat: Grassland, lawns, paths, verges, very common everywhere
ribwort-plantain.summary: Rosette of narrow, strongly ribbed leaves and short dark flower heads on long stalks. A traditional first-aid plant for stings and minor cuts.

greater-plantain.name: Greater plantain
greater-plantain.habitat: Trampled ground: paths, gateways, farm tracks, lawns
greater-plantain.summary: Flat rosette of broad oval leaves with parallel veins, thriving on trampled paths. Edible greens and a traditional poultice plant.

yarrow.name: Yarrow
yarrow.summary: Feathery, finely divided aromatic leaves and flat-topped clusters of small white or pink flowers. A traditional wound herb.

common-sorrel.name: Common sorrel
common-sorrel.summary: Arrow-shaped leaves with a sharp lemony taste and backward-pointing lobes clasping the stem. Edible in moderation.

wood-sorrel.name: Wood sorrel
wood-sorrel.habitat: Shady, damp woodland floors, mossy banks and tree bases
wood-sorrel.summary: Clover-like trefoil leaves that fold up at night and a delicate white flower with lilac veins. Pleasantly sour, eat a little.

hawthorn.name: Hawthorn
hawthorn.season: Young leaves Apr–May; flowers May; haws (berries) Sep–Nov
hawthorn.habitat: Hedgerows everywhere, scrub, woodland edges, upland valleys
hawthorn.summary: Thorny hedgerow shrub with deeply lobed leaves, white "may" blossom and clusters of dark red haws in autumn.

blackberry.name: Bramble (blackberry)
blackberry.season: Young shoots Apr–Jun; berries late Jul–Sep (traditionally not after Michaelmas, 29 Sep, when they go mouldy)
blackberry.habitat: Hedges, woodland, scrub, waste ground, everywhere
blackberry.summary: Arching, prickly stems with leaves of 3–5 toothed leaflets and familiar black berries. Very safe and very common.

raspberry.name: Wild raspberry
raspberry.habitat: Woodland clearings, heaths, upland scrub, especially in the north and west
raspberry.summary: Upright canes with fine bristles, leaves white underneath, and red berries that pull off leaving a hollow cup.

elder.name: Elder
elder.habitat: Hedgerows, woodland edges, waste ground, around rabbit warrens and old buildings
elder.summary: Fast-growing shrub with pinnate leaves, flat creamy flower heads and drooping clusters of tiny black berries. Flowers and cooked berries are edible.

dog-rose.name: Dog rose (rosehips)
dog-rose.season: Flowers Jun–Jul; hips Sep–Dec (sweeter after frost)
dog-rose.summary: Scrambling rose with hooked prickles, pale pink flowers and bright red oval hips, very rich in vitamin C.

blackthorn.name: Blackthorn (sloe)
blackthorn.season: Flowers Mar–Apr (before leaves); sloes Sep–Nov (best after frost)
blackthorn.habitat: Hedgerows, scrub, woodland edges, coastal cliffs
blackthorn.summary: Dense, black-barked thorny shrub with white blossom before the leaves, and blue-black, bloom-covered sloes.

bilberry.name: Bilberry
bilberry.habitat: Acid heaths, moorland, upland and pine/oak woods
bilberry.summary: Low, bright-green shrub on moorland with small oval leaves and blue-black berries with a flat crown. Excellent food.

wild-strawberry.name: Wild strawberry
wild-strawberry.habitat: Woodland edges, banks, dry grassland, railway cuttings, on chalk especially
wild-strawberry.summary: Tiny strawberries on a low plant with three-toothed leaflets and white five-petalled flowers.

crab-apple.name: Crab apple
crab-apple.summary: Small tree with apple blossom and small, very sour yellow-green apples. Cook them; they are full of pectin.

wild-cherry.name: Wild cherry
wild-cherry.summary: Tall tree with shiny red-brown bark peeling in horizontal bands and small dark red cherries.

hazel.name: Hazel
hazel.summary: Multi-stemmed shrub with round, soft, toothed leaves, yellow "lamb's tail" catkins and edible nuts in frilly husks.

sweet-chestnut.name: Sweet chestnut
sweet-chestnut.habitat: Woods and parks, especially on sandy soils in southern England
sweet-chestnut.summary: Large tree with long, glossy, saw-toothed leaves and very spiny cases holding brown chestnuts. Roast them; do not confuse with poisonous conkers.

beech.name: Beech
beech.season: Young leaves Apr–May; beechmast (nuts) Sep–Oct, heavy crops only some years
beech.habitat: Woods on chalk and limestone, plantations, parks
beech.summary: Smooth grey-barked tree with oval wavy-edged leaves and small triangular nuts in bristly husks.

silver-birch.name: Silver birch
silver-birch.season: Sap rises Mar (2–3 weeks before leaves open); bark all year
silver-birch.habitat: Heaths, open woods, upland, waste ground; a pioneer tree everywhere
silver-birch.summary: White papery bark with dark diamond marks, and drooping twigs. Bark is the best natural UK tinder and the sap is drinkable.

scots-pine.name: Scots pine
scots-pine.season: Needles all year; resin all year
scots-pine.habitat: Native in the Scottish Highlands, planted widely across the UK on heaths and sandy soils
scots-pine.summary: Tall pine with orange-red flaky upper bark and paired blue-green needles. Resin-soaked "fatwood" is excellent fire starter.

norway-spruce.name: Norway spruce
norway-spruce.season: Young tips Apr–Jun; needles all year
norway-spruce.summary: The Christmas tree: single, four-sided sharp needles on small pegs, and long hanging cones. Fresh green tips are edible.

burdock.name: Lesser burdock
burdock.season: Roots of first-year plants Sep–Mar; young stems May–Jun
burdock.habitat: Woodland edges, waste ground, verges, field margins
burdock.summary: Huge rhubarb-like leaves, woolly underneath, and purple thistle-like flowers that become hooked burrs. Roots are edible cooked.

chickweed.name: Common chickweed
chickweed.habitat: Gardens, field edges, disturbed ground, farmyards
chickweed.summary: Sprawling, mat-forming plant with small oval leaves, tiny white star flowers and a single line of hairs down the stem.

common-mallow.name: Common mallow
common-mallow.habitat: Verges, waste ground, field edges, coastal banks
common-mallow.summary: Bushy plant with round, shallowly lobed leaves and pink-purple flowers striped with darker veins. Leaves and seed "cheeses" are edible.

red-clover.name: Red clover
red-clover.summary: Familiar clover with three oval leaflets, each with a pale crescent, and round pinkish-purple flower heads.

hairy-bittercress.name: Hairy bittercress
hairy-bittercress.season: Leaves most of the year (best Jan–May)
hairy-bittercress.summary: Small rosette of round-leafleted leaves with a peppery cress taste and tiny white four-petalled flowers.

watercress.name: Watercress
watercress.habitat: Shallow, clear, flowing streams and ditches, especially on chalk
watercress.summary: Floating and creeping aquatic plant with pinnate leaves of rounded leaflets and a hot, peppery taste. Wild plants must be cooked.

sea-beet.name: Sea beet
sea-beet.habitat: Coastal shingle, sea walls, cliffs and saltmarsh edges
sea-beet.summary: The wild ancestor of beetroot and chard: glossy, thick, dark green leaves on the shore. An excellent wild spinach.

samphire.name: Marsh samphire
samphire.summary: Small, jointed, succulent green stems like tiny cacti, growing in tidal mud. Salty and crunchy.

water-mint.name: Water mint
water-mint.habitat: Wet ground beside rivers, ponds, marshes and ditches
water-mint.summary: Strongly mint-scented plant of wet places with hairy, toothed leaves and round lilac flower heads.

meadowsweet.name: Meadowsweet
meadowsweet.habitat: Damp meadows, ditches, riverbanks, wet woodland
meadowsweet.summary: Tall plant of wet places with frothy cream flower clusters smelling of almond and honey. A traditional source of salicylates.

lime-tree.name: Common lime (linden)
lime-tree.summary: Large tree with heart-shaped, lopsided leaves that are a pleasant salad green when young, and fragrant flowers for tea.

oak.name: English oak (acorns)
oak.habitat: Woodland, hedgerows and parkland throughout the UK
oak.summary: Broad, long-lived tree with lobed leaves and acorns. Acorns are a big calorie source, but only after leaching out the bitter tannins.

willow.name: Willow
willow.season: Bark best in spring; all year
willow.habitat: Riverbanks, wet ground, fens and lakesides
willow.summary: Trees of wet places with long narrow leaves (or oval in goat willow) and catkins. Flexible rods for weaving; the bark contains salicin.

rowan.name: Rowan
rowan.habitat: Uplands, moorland edges, rocky ground, also widely planted in streets
rowan.summary: Small tree with feather-like leaves of toothed leaflets and heavy clusters of orange-red berries. Berries must be cooked.

bracken.name: Bracken
bracken.season: All year; dead brown fronds Oct–Mar
bracken.habitat: Hillsides, heaths, woodland and moorland across the UK; often vast stands
bracken.summary: Tall, tough fern covering hillsides. Do not eat it, but dead brown fronds are good tinder and insulating bedding.

horsetail.name: Field horsetail
horsetail.season: Fertile shoots Mar–Apr; green stems Apr–Oct
horsetail.habitat: Damp ground, field edges, verges, waste ground
horsetail.summary: Primitive plant of jointed, hollow green stems with whorls of needle-like branches. Gritty with silica: useful as a scourer, not as food.

comfrey.name: Comfrey
comfrey.habitat: Riverbanks, ditches, damp verges, field edges
comfrey.summary: Big, bristly-hairy leaves and drooping clusters of bell flowers. Known as "knitbone": for external use only.

sphagnum.name: Sphagnum moss
sphagnum.habitat: Bogs, wet moorland, wet heath, wet hollows in upland woods
sphagnum.summary: Soft, very absorbent bog moss in green, red or golden cushions. Used as a wound dressing in WW1; also marks dangerous bog.

reedmace.name: Bulrush (reedmace)
reedmace.season: Shoots Apr–Jun; green flower spikes Jun; pollen Jun–Jul; down Oct–Mar; rhizomes autumn–winter
reedmace.habitat: Shallow water at the edges of ponds, lakes, canals and ditches
reedmace.summary: Tall waterside plant with strap-like leaves and the iconic brown "sausage" seed head. A food source, and its fluffy down is excellent tinder.

gorse.name: Gorse
gorse.habitat: Heaths, rough grassland, cliffs, moorland edges
gorse.summary: Dense, very spiny evergreen shrub with coconut-scented yellow pea flowers. Dead gorse burns ferociously.

heather.name: Heather (ling)
heather.season: Flowers Jul–Sep; all year as bedding and fuel
heather.habitat: Moorland and heath on acid soils; vast areas in the uplands
heather.summary: Low woody shrub with tiny scale-like leaves and pink-purple flower spikes covering moorland. Useful bedding, fuel and tea.

thistle.name: Spear thistle
thistle.summary: Spiny-leaved thistle with purple flower heads. The peeled stems are edible, and the dry down helps catch a flame.

self-heal.name: Self-heal
self-heal.summary: Low creeping plant with square stems and dense purple flower heads. Edible and traditionally applied to small wounds.

ground-elder.name: Ground elder
ground-elder.habitat: Gardens, shady verges, woodland edges near habitation
ground-elder.summary: Invasive carpeting plant whose leaves are divided into three groups of three. Young leaves are edible, but it is a carrot-family plant, so identify with extreme care.

cow-parsley.name: Cow parsley
cow-parsley.habitat: Road verges, hedgerows and woodland edges everywhere, in huge drifts in May
cow-parsley.summary: Lacy white umbels lining every lane in spring. Technically edible, but almost identical to deadly hemlock and fool's parsley: treat it as off-limits.

common-hogweed.name: Common hogweed
common-hogweed.summary: Large, coarse umbellifer with broad, hairy, lobed leaves and big flat white umbels. Its sap can burn skin in sunlight.

dogwood.name: Common dogwood
dogwood.season: Flowers Jun–Jul; berries Aug–Oct; red twigs in winter
dogwood.habitat: Hedgerows and scrub on chalk and limestone, woodland edges
dogwood.summary: Hedgerow shrub with oval leaves whose veins curve towards the tip, flat white flower heads, and bitter black berries. Not edible.

alexanders.name: Alexanders
alexanders.season: Leaves Oct–Apr (green right through winter); flowers Mar–Jun; black seeds Jun–Sep
alexanders.habitat: Coastal hedge banks, cliff tops, verges and waste ground near the sea, often around old castles and abbeys; mainly southern and eastern coasts, spreading inland along roads
alexanders.summary: Glossy, celery-scented umbellifer with leaves in threes and yellow-green flower heads, lush when little else is green. Edible, but it belongs to the family that includes deadly hemlock water-dropwort.

rock-samphire.name: Rock samphire
rock-samphire.season: Leaves Apr–Oct (best May–Jul, before flowering); flowers Jun–Oct
rock-samphire.habitat: Sea cliffs, rocks, sea walls, harbour walls and shingle just above the tide, mainly on the south and west coasts of Britain
rock-samphire.summary: Bushy, grey-green coastal plant with fleshy, cylindrical leaflets and a strong resinous smell. Edible cooked or pickled; the cliffs it grows on are the real danger.

sea-purslane.name: Sea purslane
sea-purslane.habitat: Salt marshes, especially fringing creeks and pools covered by high tides; south, east and west coasts of Britain
sea-purslane.summary: Low, silvery-grey shrub lining saltmarsh creeks, with small, fleshy, mealy leaves that taste salty and crunchy. Edible raw or cooked, but mind the tide and the mud.

scurvy-grass.name: Common scurvygrass
scurvy-grass.season: Leaves all year (best Feb–Jun); flowers Apr–Aug
scurvy-grass.habitat: Salt marshes, sea cliffs, sea walls and coastal rocks; also mountain ledges. The related Danish scurvygrass lines salted main roads and motorways inland.
scurvy-grass.summary: Low coastal plant with fleshy, glossy, heart- to kidney-shaped leaves and small white four-petalled flowers. Hot and bitter, but rich in vitamin C, which gave it its name.

sea-buckthorn.name: Sea buckthorn
sea-buckthorn.habitat: Coastal sand dunes and sea cliffs, native mainly on the east coast of England; widely planted on dunes, road verges and in landscaping elsewhere
sea-buckthorn.summary: Thorny, silvery-leaved shrub covered in dense clusters of bright orange berries. Very sour but edible, and one of the richest wild sources of vitamin C.

wild-marjoram.name: Wild marjoram
wild-marjoram.habitat: Dry grassland, scrub, banks, quarries and roadsides on chalk and limestone; commonest in southern England, scattered further north
wild-marjoram.summary: Bushy aromatic herb with oval leaves in opposite pairs and clusters of small pink-purple flowers. It is wild oregano: a flavouring and a traditional tea.

wild-thyme.name: Wild thyme
wild-thyme.habitat: Short, dry grassland on chalk and limestone, heaths, sand dunes, rocky outcrops, cliff tops and mountain ledges throughout the UK
wild-thyme.summary: Low creeping mat of tiny paired leaves with rounded heads of pink-purple flowers, smelling of thyme. A flavouring and traditional tea.

fat-hen.name: Fat hen
fat-hen.habitat: Disturbed, rich ground: field edges, gardens, allotments, farmyards, manure heaps and building sites
fat-hen.summary: Common weed with goosefoot-shaped leaves dusted with a white, mealy bloom. A nourishing cooked green, like spinach, eaten in Britain since prehistory.

ground-ivy.name: Ground ivy
ground-ivy.habitat: Woodland edges, hedge banks, shady grassland, lawns and gardens, in damp or shady places throughout the UK
ground-ivy.summary: Low, creeping mint-family plant with round, scalloped leaves and violet-blue flowers in spring. Strongly aromatic; used as a herb, a tea and once to flavour ale. Not related to ivy.

wood-avens.name: Wood avens
wood-avens.season: Leaves Mar–Oct; flowers May–Aug; roots best Mar–Apr
wood-avens.habitat: Woodland edges, hedgerows, shady gardens and path sides; common almost everywhere in lowland Britain
wood-avens.summary: Woodland weed with small yellow five-petalled flowers, hooked burr-like seed heads and roots that smell of cloves. The root is a spice and a traditional remedy.

japanese-knotweed.name: Japanese knotweed
japanese-knotweed.season: Shoots Mar–May; leaves May–Oct; flowers Aug–Oct; dead canes stand all winter
japanese-knotweed.habitat: Riverbanks, railway lines, roadsides, waste ground, gardens and car parks throughout the UK, especially in towns and along rivers
japanese-knotweed.summary: Dense thickets of bamboo-like, red-speckled canes with shield-shaped leaves. Young shoots are edible, like rhubarb, but stands are often sprayed with weedkiller and the law on spreading it is strict.

himalayan-balsam.name: Himalayan balsam
himalayan-balsam.season: Shoots Apr–May; flowers Jun–Oct; seed pods Jul–Oct
himalayan-balsam.habitat: Riverbanks, streamsides, wet woodland, ditches and damp waste ground throughout the UK, often in dense stands
himalayan-balsam.summary: Tall, pink-flowered annual with hollow reddish stems and seed pods that explode when touched, smothering riverbanks. Flowers and seeds are edible; you must not spread the seeds.

rosebay-willowherb.name: Rosebay willowherb
rosebay-willowherb.season: Young shoots Apr–May; leaves May–Aug; flowers Jun–Sep; seed down Aug–Oct
rosebay-willowherb.habitat: Woodland clearings, felled and burnt ground, railway banks, waste ground, heaths and road verges throughout the UK
rosebay-willowherb.summary: Tall spikes of magenta flowers over long, narrow leaves, colonising cleared and burnt ground. Young shoots and leaves are edible, and the silky seed down helps a spark catch.

chicory.name: Chicory
chicory.season: Leaves Mar–Jun; flowers Jul–Oct; roots Sep–Mar
chicory.habitat: Road verges, field edges, rough grassland and waste ground, mostly on chalk and limestone in southern and eastern England; scattered elsewhere
chicory.summary: Stiff, branching plant with sky-blue, dandelion-like flowers along the stems. The leaves are a bitter salad and the roasted root is a classic coffee substitute.

sheeps-sorrel.name: Sheep's sorrel
sheeps-sorrel.habitat: Acid soils: heaths, sandy grassland, moorland, cliff tops, old walls and gravelly ground
sheeps-sorrel.summary: Small, slender sorrel with lemon-sour, arrow-shaped leaves whose basal lobes point outwards. Edible raw in small amounts, like common sorrel.

juniper.name: Juniper
juniper.season: Evergreen; ripe blue-black berries Sep–Nov (green unripe berries all year)
juniper.habitat: Chalk downland in southern England; limestone hills, moorland and native pinewoods in northern England and Scotland; declining and local
juniper.summary: Prickly evergreen conifer with needles in whorls of three and blue-black, bloomed berries. The berries are a flavouring (the main taste of gin), not a food to eat by the handful.

cowberry.name: Cowberry
cowberry.season: Flowers May–Jul; berries Aug–Oct, often hanging on into winter
cowberry.habitat: Upland moors, heaths and pine and birch woods on acid soil, mainly in Scotland, northern England, Wales and the Peak District
cowberry.summary: Low evergreen shrub with small, glossy, leathery leaves and clusters of shiny red berries. Sharp but edible, much like cranberry.

sweet-violet.name: Sweet violet
sweet-violet.habitat: Hedge banks, woodland edges, churchyards, scrub and shady verges, mostly on chalky or rich soils in England and Wales
sweet-violet.summary: Low plant with heart-shaped leaves and sweetly scented violet or white flowers in early spring. Flowers and young leaves are edible.

walnut.name: Walnut
walnut.habitat: Parks, large gardens, field corners, old estates, hedgerows and riverbanks, mainly in southern and central England
walnut.summary: Large, spreading tree with aromatic pinnate leaves and smooth green fruits holding the familiar walnut. The nuts are a rich food; the husks stain skin and are not eaten.

sycamore.name: Sycamore
sycamore.season: Sap rises Feb–Mar; leaves Apr–Oct; winged seeds Aug–Oct
sycamore.habitat: Everywhere: woods, hedgerows, parks, towns, upland farms and exposed coasts; often the only tree around northern and Scottish farmsteads
sycamore.summary: Common large tree with five-lobed leaves and paired, winged "helicopter" seeds. Its sap can be tapped in late winter for a drink or syrup; the seeds are poisonous and must not be eaten.

st-johns-wort.name: Perforate St John's-wort
st-johns-wort.habitat: Grassland, open woods, scrub, verges, railway banks and waste ground, especially on chalk and limestone; throughout most of the UK
st-johns-wort.summary: Upright plant with bright yellow flowers whose leaves are peppered with see-through dots. A well-known herbal remedy that dangerously interferes with many medicines.

valerian.name: Common valerian
valerian.season: Leaves Apr–Oct; flowers Jun–Aug; roots Sep–Oct
valerian.habitat: Damp grassland, fens, riverbanks, ditches and wet woodland rides; also dry chalk grassland; throughout the UK
valerian.summary: Tall plant of damp places with pinnate leaves and rounded heads of small pale pink flowers. Its strong-smelling root is a traditional sedative, and it grows beside deadly water-dropwort.

dogs-mercury.name: Dog's mercury
dogs-mercury.season: Shoots from Jan; flowers Feb–Apr; leaves until autumn
dogs-mercury.habitat: Shady deciduous woodland, especially old woods on chalk and limestone, and shady hedge banks; carpets the ground, often with bluebells and wild garlic
dogs-mercury.summary: Low woodland carpet plant with paired, toothed leaves and tiny green flowers in early spring. Poisonous, even cooked; it grows among wild garlic and has been eaten by mistake for other greens.

stinking-hellebore.name: Stinking hellebore
stinking-hellebore.habitat: Woods, scrub and banks on chalk and limestone in southern and western England and Wales; widely planted in gardens
stinking-hellebore.summary: Evergreen woodland plant with dark, hand-shaped leaves and clusters of nodding, pale green bell flowers rimmed with maroon. All parts are poisonous and the sap irritates skin.

mistletoe.name: Mistletoe
mistletoe.habitat: High in the branches of apple trees, limes, poplars, hawthorns and other broadleaves, mainly in southern and central England and the Welsh borders, especially old orchards
mistletoe.summary: Round, evergreen balls of forked yellow-green stems in tree branches, with sticky white berries in winter. Berries, leaves and stems are poisonous.

box.name: Box
box.habitat: Native on a few chalk and limestone slopes in southern England (such as Box Hill in Surrey); planted everywhere as hedging, edging and topiary in gardens, churchyards and estates
box.summary: Dense evergreen shrub with small, glossy, oval leaves in pairs, used for hedges and topiary. Leaves and bark are poisonous; the crushed leaves smell of cat urine.

spurge-laurel.name: Spurge laurel
spurge-laurel.season: Evergreen; flowers Jan–Apr; black berries Jun–Jul
spurge-laurel.habitat: Woods and scrub on chalk, limestone and clay, mainly in England and Wales, often under beech
spurge-laurel.summary: Low evergreen shrub with glossy leaves bunched at the top of bare stems, small green flowers in winter and black berries in summer. All parts are very poisonous and the sap blisters skin.

petty-spurge.name: Petty spurge
petty-spurge.season: Flowers most of the year (mainly Apr–Nov)
petty-spurge.habitat: Gardens, allotments, flower beds, paving cracks, field edges and waste ground; very common
petty-spurge.summary: Small, hairless garden weed with round leaves and tiny green flower heads, full of white milky sap that burns skin and severely damages eyes. Other spurges are similar.

marsh-marigold.name: Marsh marigold
marsh-marigold.habitat: Marshes, wet meadows, fens, wet woodland, ditches and the edges of streams and ponds throughout the UK
marsh-marigold.summary: Lush waterside plant with large, glossy, kidney-shaped leaves and big golden buttercup-like flowers in spring. Poisonous raw, and its juice can blister skin.

cotoneaster.name: Cotoneaster
cotoneaster.habitat: Gardens, car parks, supermarket and roadside landscaping, walls; escaped onto limestone cliffs, quarries, railway banks and dunes
cotoneaster.summary: Common landscaping shrubs, from flat herringbone ground cover to small trees, covered in red berries through autumn and winter. The berries are mildly poisonous, and several species are invasive.

herb-paris.name: Herb Paris
herb-paris.habitat: Damp, ancient woodland on chalk, limestone or other lime-rich soils, often with dog's mercury; scattered across Britain, local
herb-paris.summary: A single stem with four broad leaves in a cross and one spidery green flower, followed by a single shiny blue-black berry. The berry and the whole plant are poisonous.

solomons-seal.name: Solomon's seal
solomons-seal.season: Shoots Apr; flowers May–Jun; berries Aug–Sep
solomons-seal.habitat: Old woodland on chalk and limestone (native but local, mainly southern England); very common in gardens and as a garden escape
solomons-seal.summary: Arching stems with two rows of oval leaves and small greenish-white bells hanging beneath, followed by blue-black berries. All parts, especially the berries, are poisonous.

snowdrop.name: Snowdrop
snowdrop.season: Leaves Dec–Apr; flowers Jan–Mar; dies back by late spring
snowdrop.habitat: Damp woodland, stream banks, churchyards, parks and old estates; widely naturalised from gardens
snowdrop.summary: Familiar late-winter flower: nodding white bells with green markings above narrow grey-green leaves. The bulbs are poisonous and look like small onions.

meadow-saffron.name: Meadow saffron
meadow-saffron.season: Leaves Mar–Jun (with a seed capsule in the middle); flowers Aug–Oct with no leaves
meadow-saffron.habitat: Damp meadows and open woods on limestone and clay, mainly in southern and central England and the Welsh borders; scarce in the wild but common in gardens and churchyards
meadow-saffron.summary: Pale pink-purple crocus-like flowers in autumn with no leaves; broad, glossy, tulip-like leaves in spring. Deadly: the spring leaves have been mistaken for wild garlic.

tansy.name: Tansy
tansy.habitat: Roadsides, riverbanks, waste ground, rough grassland and field edges throughout the UK
tansy.summary: Tall plant with fern-like, strongly aromatic leaves and flat-topped clusters of yellow button flowers. Once used as a herb, but it contains thujone and is poisonous.

wild-parsnip.name: Wild parsnip
wild-parsnip.habitat: Chalk and limestone grassland, road verges, field edges, railway banks and waste ground, mainly in southern and eastern England
wild-parsnip.summary: Tall umbellifer with flat-topped yellow flower heads, once-divided leaves and a parsnip smell. Its sap burns skin in sunlight, and the leaves are no food: leave it alone.

wood-anemone.name: Wood anemone
wood-anemone.habitat: Ancient deciduous woodland and old hedge banks; in the west and north also open hillsides and meadows; carpets the woodland floor in spring
wood-anemone.summary: Spring woodland carpets of white, star-like flowers above deeply cut leaves in threes. Poisonous: don't confuse it with wood sorrel or wild garlic growing in the same woods.

greater-celandine.name: Greater celandine
greater-celandine.habitat: Old walls, hedge banks, waysides and waste ground, usually near houses, villages and churches
greater-celandine.summary: Leafy, grey-green poppy-family plant with small four-petalled yellow flowers and bright orange sap. Poisonous; the sap irritates skin, and herbal use has damaged livers.

hemp-agrimony.name: Hemp-agrimony
hemp-agrimony.habitat: Riverbanks, ditches, fens, marshes, damp woodland rides and clearings, and coastal cliffs; throughout lowland Britain
hemp-agrimony.summary: Tall waterside plant with leaves split like a hand into 3–5 toothed lobes and fluffy, dull pink flower heads loved by butterflies. It damages the liver; not a herb to use.

snowberry.name: Snowberry
snowberry.habitat: Hedges, woodland edges, shrubberies, estates, parks and railway banks; planted for game cover and widely naturalised
snowberry.summary: Thicket-forming shrub with small oval leaves and round, marble-like white berries that last into winter. The berries are mildly poisonous.

hemlock.name: Hemlock
hemlock.season: Leaves from late winter; flowers Jun–Jul; dead stems stand into winter
hemlock.habitat: Damp ground: ditches, riverbanks, rough verges, field edges, waste ground and rubbish tips
hemlock.summary: Tall, smooth carrot-family plant with purple-blotched stems, lacy leaves and a mousy smell. Every part can kill.

hemlock-water-dropwort.name: Hemlock water-dropwort
hemlock-water-dropwort.season: Leaves from Nov (green through winter); flowers Jun–Jul
hemlock-water-dropwort.habitat: Wet ground beside streams, rivers, ditches, canals and marshes, especially in the south and west of Britain
hemlock-water-dropwort.summary: Probably the UK's most poisonous plant: a lush, celery-scented waterside umbellifer whose finger-like roots kill quickly.

fools-parsley.name: Fool's parsley
fools-parsley.summary: Small garden umbellifer like flat-leaf parsley but with long, hanging "beards" of bracts under each small umbel. Poisonous.

giant-hogweed.name: Giant hogweed
giant-hogweed.habitat: Riverbanks, waste ground, railway lines and roadsides, spreading along watercourses
giant-hogweed.summary: Enormous umbellifer (3–5 m) with purple-blotched bristly stems and umbels up to 80 cm across. Its sap causes severe burns in sunlight.

cowbane.name: Cowbane
cowbane.habitat: Shallow water and swamps by lakes, fens and ditches; local (Norfolk Broads, Cheshire/Shropshire meres, parts of Scotland and Ireland)
cowbane.summary: Rare but extremely poisonous waterside umbellifer whose hollow rootstock is divided into chambers. Related to the North American water hemlocks.

foxglove.name: Foxglove
foxglove.season: Leaf rosettes all year; flowers Jun–Sep (second year)
foxglove.habitat: Woodland clearings, heaths, hedge banks, acid soils, gardens
foxglove.summary: Tall spikes of purple tubular bell flowers spotted inside. The soft leaves are deadly, and the rosettes can be confused with comfrey or borage.

deadly-nightshade.name: Deadly nightshade
deadly-nightshade.habitat: Woodland edges and clearings, scrub, old quarries and ruins on chalk and limestone (uncommon, mainly south and east England)
deadly-nightshade.summary: Bushy plant with dull, bell-shaped purple-brown flowers and glossy black, cherry-like berries sitting in a green star. A few berries can kill a child.

black-nightshade.name: Black nightshade
black-nightshade.summary: Low weedy plant with small white star flowers with yellow centres and clusters of small, dull black berries. Treat it as poisonous.

bittersweet.name: Bittersweet
bittersweet.habitat: Hedgerows, scrub, woodland edges, riverbanks, reedbeds
bittersweet.summary: Scrambling climber with purple star flowers with a yellow beak, and oval berries turning green to orange to bright red. Poisonous.

lords-and-ladies.name: Lords-and-ladies
lords-and-ladies.season: Leaves Jan–May; flower hood Apr–May; red berries Jul–Sep
lords-and-ladies.habitat: Shady woodland, hedgerow bases and banks, often among wild garlic and bluebells
lords-and-ladies.summary: Arrow-shaped, glossy, often dark-spotted leaves in woodland, then a hooded flower and a spike of bright orange-red berries. Very painful poison.

lily-of-the-valley.name: Lily of the valley
lily-of-the-valley.season: Leaves Apr–Jun; flowers May–Jun; red berries Aug–Sep
lily-of-the-valley.habitat: Dry woods on limestone (local and scattered in the wild); garden escapes near habitation
lily-of-the-valley.summary: Paired, broad, elliptical leaves with tiny scented white bell flowers on one side of a stalk. A garlic lookalike that can stop the heart.

yew.name: Yew
yew.habitat: Churchyards, chalk downland woods, gardens, old woodland
yew.summary: Dark evergreen with flat needles in two rows and red cup-shaped berries. Everything except the red flesh is deadly, including the seed inside it.

holly.name: Holly
holly.summary: Evergreen with glossy, spiny leaves and bright red berries. The berries are poisonous, but the dead leaves and branches make good fuel.

ivy.name: Ivy
ivy.season: Evergreen; flowers Sep–Nov; black berries Jan–Apr
ivy.habitat: Woods, hedges, walls, tree trunks, everywhere
ivy.summary: Evergreen climber with glossy lobed leaves and round black berry clusters in late winter. Poisonous to eat; sap can irritate skin.

privet.name: Wild privet
privet.habitat: Hedgerows and scrub on chalk; garden hedges (garden privet is a close relative)
privet.summary: Hedge shrub with small, smooth, oval leaves in pairs, strong-smelling white flower spikes and clusters of shiny black berries. Poisonous.

ragwort.name: Common ragwort
ragwort.habitat: Pasture, verges, sand dunes, waste ground
ragwort.summary: Yellow daisy-flowered plant in flat-topped clusters with ragged, deeply cut leaves. Toxic to the liver; do not eat or handle with bare hands for long.

monkshood.name: Monkshood
monkshood.habitat: Shady stream banks in south-west England and Wales; gardens and garden escapes
monkshood.summary: Tall spikes of deep blue-purple hooded flowers above deeply divided leaves. The UK's most toxic garden plant; poison can be absorbed through the skin.

black-bryony.name: Black bryony
black-bryony.habitat: Hedgerows, woodland edges, scrub, in southern Britain
black-bryony.summary: Twining climber with glossy, heart-shaped leaves and strings of shiny red berries in hedges in autumn. Poisonous.

white-bryony.name: White bryony
white-bryony.habitat: Hedgerows and scrub, mainly in England
white-bryony.summary: Climbing plant with ivy-like lobed leaves, curly tendrils and clusters of red berries. The huge white root is very poisonous.

spindle.name: Spindle
spindle.habitat: Hedgerows, woodland edges, chalk and limestone scrub
spindle.summary: Hedgerow shrub with striking four-lobed bright pink fruits that open to show orange seeds. Poisonous.

laburnum.name: Laburnum
laburnum.habitat: Gardens, parks, streets; occasionally escaped into hedges
laburnum.summary: Small garden tree with long hanging chains of yellow pea flowers and pea-like seed pods. Seeds are seriously poisonous.

daffodil.name: Wild daffodil
daffodil.habitat: Damp woods and meadows; garden daffodils everywhere along verges
daffodil.summary: Familiar yellow trumpet flowers. The bulbs have been mistaken for onions and the leaves for wild garlic, with poisonous results.

bluebell.name: Bluebell
bluebell.habitat: Ancient broadleaf woodland, hedge banks, and in the west on bracken hillsides
bluebell.summary: Carpets of nodding blue-violet bells in spring woods. Poisonous, legally protected, and its narrow leaves grow among wild garlic.

rhododendron.name: Rhododendron
rhododendron.habitat: Woods, moorland edges, estates, especially on acid soils in the west and Scotland
rhododendron.summary: Invasive evergreen shrub with large leathery leaves and big purple flower clusters. Every part is toxic, including honey made from it.

cherry-laurel.name: Cherry laurel
cherry-laurel.summary: Glossy evergreen hedge shrub with large leathery leaves smelling of almonds when crushed, and cherry-like black fruit. Leaves and seeds release cyanide.

horse-chestnut.name: Horse chestnut (conkers)
horse-chestnut.summary: Large tree with big hand-shaped leaves and glossy brown conkers in thick, lightly spiked cases. Conkers are poisonous; don't confuse them with sweet chestnuts.

buttercup.name: Meadow buttercup
buttercup.summary: Glossy yellow cup-shaped flowers on tall stems over deeply divided leaves. Blistering juice; never eat buttercups.

lesser-celandine.name: Lesser celandine
lesser-celandine.habitat: Damp woods, hedge banks, stream sides, shady grass
lesser-celandine.summary: Early spring carpets of glossy, heart-shaped leaves and shiny yellow star-like flowers. Raw plant is irritant; it grows among wild garlic.

scarlet-pimpernel.name: Scarlet pimpernel
scarlet-pimpernel.habitat: Arable fields, gardens, dunes, waste ground
scarlet-pimpernel.summary: Low, sprawling plant with small orange-red flowers, similar to chickweed when not in flower. Mildly poisonous.

guelder-rose.name: Guelder rose
guelder-rose.habitat: Damp woods, hedgerows, fens and stream sides
guelder-rose.summary: Shrub with maple-like three-lobed leaves, lacecap white flowers and hanging bunches of translucent red berries. Poisonous raw.

buckthorn.name: Buckthorn
buckthorn.habitat: Hedgerows, scrub and fen edges on chalk, limestone and fen peat (England and Wales)
buckthorn.summary: Thorny shrub with oval, finely toothed leaves with curved veins, and clusters of black berries that are a violent purgative.

yellow-iris.name: Yellow iris
yellow-iris.habitat: Pond and river margins, marshes, wet woods, ditches
yellow-iris.summary: Waterside plant with sword-shaped leaves and big yellow iris flowers. Poisonous; its leaves resemble bulrush and sweet flag.

fools-watercress.name: Fool's watercress
fools-watercress.habitat: Streams, ditches and wet mud, often with watercress
fools-watercress.summary: Creeping waterside umbellifer that looks like watercress but has toothed leaflets and tiny white umbels. Not worth the risk.

wild-celery.name: Wild celery
wild-celery.habitat: Damp ground near the sea: saltmarsh edges, ditches, riverbanks
wild-celery.summary: Strong celery-scented coastal umbellifer. Wild celery is edible to experts, but deadly hemlock water-dropwort also smells of celery.

honeysuckle.name: Honeysuckle
honeysuckle.season: Flowers Jun–Sep; red berries Aug–Oct; bark all year
honeysuckle.habitat: Woodland, hedgerows and scrub, twining up trees and shrubs
honeysuckle.summary: Twining climber with sweet-scented cream and pink trumpet flowers and clusters of red berries. Berries are mildly poisonous; the papery bark is superb tinder.

clematis.name: Traveller's joy (old man's beard)
clematis.season: Flowers Jul–Sep; fluffy seed heads Sep–Feb; bark all year
clematis.habitat: Hedgerows, woodland edges and scrub on chalk and limestone, mainly in southern England and Wales
clematis.summary: Woody climber smothering hedges with fluffy grey-white seed heads in autumn and winter. Poisonous sap, but its shaggy bark makes an excellent tinder nest.

death-cap.name: Death cap
death-cap.habitat: Broadleaf woodland, especially under oak and beech; also parks with those trees; mainly southern Britain
death-cap.summary: Olive-green to yellowish cap, white gills, a skirt-like ring and a bag-like volva at the base. Causes most of the world's mushroom deaths.

destroying-angel.name: Destroying angel
destroying-angel.habitat: Woodland on acid soils, under birch, pine and beech; commonest in Scotland and northern England
destroying-angel.summary: Pure white mushroom with a ring, a shaggy stem and a sac-like volva. As deadly as the death cap.

fly-agaric.name: Fly agaric
fly-agaric.habitat: Under birch and pine (sometimes spruce), on heaths and in woods
fly-agaric.summary: The fairy-tale toadstool: scarlet cap with white warty flecks, white gills and a ring. Poisonous and hallucinogenic; a close relative of the deadly death cap.

panther-cap.name: Panther cap
panther-cap.habitat: Broadleaf woods (beech, oak) and sometimes conifers, especially on chalk and limestone
panther-cap.summary: Brown cap with pure white warts, white gills and a ring with a gutter-like rim to the volva. More toxic than fly agaric and can kill; a close relative of the death cap.

the-blusher.name: The blusher
the-blusher.habitat: Broadleaf and conifer woods, very common
the-blusher.summary: Common Amanita with a pinkish-brown warty cap whose flesh slowly turns pink where damaged. Toxic raw; listed here because its lookalike is the dangerous panther cap.

deadly-webcap.name: Deadly webcap
deadly-webcap.habitat: Wet, acid conifer woods with moss (pine and spruce), especially in the Scottish Highlands
deadly-webcap.summary: Tawny-orange mushroom with a pointed cap, rusty gills and faint yellow bands on the stem. Destroys the kidneys days or weeks after eating.

fools-webcap.name: Fool's webcap
fools-webcap.habitat: Broadleaf woods (oak, beech) on acid soils; rare in Britain
fools-webcap.summary: Rare orange-brown webcap, close relative of the deadly webcap, with the same delayed kidney poison.

funeral-bell.name: Funeral bell
funeral-bell.season: Mostly Sep–Dec, can appear in any month
funeral-bell.habitat: In small groups or clusters on rotting wood, especially conifer stumps and logs
funeral-bell.summary: Small brown mushroom on dead wood with a ring and rusty-brown spores. Contains the same toxins as the death cap and is easily mistaken for edible wood mushrooms.

chanterelle.name: Chanterelle
chanterelle.habitat: Mossy woodland, under beech, oak and birch, also in conifer woods; often on banks; common in Scotland and the west
chanterelle.summary: Egg-yolk yellow funnel with blunt, forked, vein-like ridges running down the stem instead of true gills, and a fruity apricot smell. Highly prized.

false-chanterelle.name: False chanterelle
false-chanterelle.habitat: Conifer woods, on needle litter, rotting wood, heathland
false-chanterelle.summary: Orange chanterelle lookalike with true, thin, crowded, repeatedly forked gills and soft flesh. Can cause stomach upset.

jack-o-lantern.name: Jack o'lantern
jack-o-lantern.habitat: Clustered on stumps or buried roots of broadleaf trees, especially oak and sweet chestnut; rare, southern England
jack-o-lantern.summary: Bright orange mushroom growing in dense clusters from wood, with true gills. A chanterelle lookalike that causes severe vomiting.

cep.name: Cep (penny bun)
cep.habitat: Broadleaf and conifer woods, especially with beech, oak, birch and pine
cep.summary: Chunky bolete with a bread-roll brown cap, sponge-like pores (not gills) that start white, and a fat stem with a fine white net pattern. A top edible.

bay-bolete.name: Bay bolete
bay-bolete.habitat: Conifer woods, also under beech and oak, on acid soils
bay-bolete.summary: Chestnut-brown bolete with a cap that is sticky when wet, and cream to yellowish pores that bruise blue-green. A good, common edible.

bitter-bolete.name: Bitter bolete
bitter-bolete.habitat: Conifer and broadleaf woods on acid soils
bitter-bolete.summary: Cep lookalike with pink-tinged pores and a dark brown net on the stem. Not dangerous, but one in the pan ruins the whole meal.

devils-bolete.name: Devil's bolete
devils-bolete.habitat: Under oak and beech on chalk and limestone, southern England; rare
devils-bolete.summary: Pale grey cap with blood-red pores and a red-netted, swollen stem; flesh turns blue. Causes severe vomiting.

field-mushroom.name: Field mushroom
field-mushroom.habitat: Grazed pasture and old grassland (horses, sheep), lawns; never in woods
field-mushroom.summary: White cap, free gills that are bright pink when young turning chocolate brown, a thin ring and no volva. Never confuse it with white Amanitas.

horse-mushroom.name: Horse mushroom
horse-mushroom.habitat: Pasture, meadows and grassy verges, sometimes in rings
horse-mushroom.summary: Large white Agaricus smelling of aniseed, with a cogwheel ring and gills that go from greyish-pink to dark brown. Easily confused with the yellow stainer.

yellow-stainer.name: Yellow stainer
yellow-stainer.habitat: Woodland edges, gardens, parks, hedgerows, grassy verges
yellow-stainer.summary: White mushroom like a field mushroom, but its flesh turns bright chrome yellow at the stem base when cut, and it smells of ink. Causes vomiting.

giant-puffball.name: Giant puffball
giant-puffball.habitat: Fields, field margins, nettle beds, hedgerows, gardens and parkland
giant-puffball.summary: A huge white ball (football-sized or bigger) with smooth leathery skin. Edible only while pure white and firm right through, like marshmallow.

common-puffball.name: Common puffball
common-puffball.habitat: Woodland floors, woodland edges and grassland, often in groups
common-puffball.summary: Small pear-shaped puffball covered in tiny pointed spines that rub off. Edible only when young, with white flesh and no gill outline inside.

common-earthball.name: Common earthball
common-earthball.habitat: Woods and heaths on acid soils, especially under birch and oak, on mossy banks
common-earthball.summary: Puffball lookalike with a thick, hard, warty yellow-brown skin and a purple-black inside even when young. Poisonous.

chicken-of-the-woods.name: Chicken of the woods
chicken-of-the-woods.habitat: Living and dead trees: oak, willow, cherry, sweet chestnut, yew, poplar
chicken-of-the-woods.summary: Bright sulphur-yellow to orange tiered brackets on trees, soft and chicken-like when young. Edible cooked, but avoid any growing on yew.

jelly-ear.name: Jelly ear
jelly-ear.season: All year, especially in wet weather in winter
jelly-ear.habitat: On dead or dying elder branches (sometimes beech, sycamore)
jelly-ear.summary: Rubbery, brown, ear-shaped fungus on elder, edible all year. Bland but safe; dries well.

oyster-mushroom.name: Oyster mushroom
oyster-mushroom.habitat: In shelf-like clusters on dead or dying broadleaf trees, especially beech
oyster-mushroom.summary: Grey-blue to brown fan-shaped caps in shelves on dead wood, with white gills running down a short side stem. Good edible.

angels-wings.name: Angel's wings
angels-wings.habitat: Rotting conifer stumps and logs, mainly in Scotland and northern England
angels-wings.summary: Thin, pure white, ear-shaped caps on conifer wood. Once eaten, it has been linked to fatal brain damage.

shaggy-inkcap.name: Shaggy inkcap
shaggy-inkcap.habitat: Grassy verges, lawns, disturbed ground, rubbish tips
shaggy-inkcap.summary: Tall white cylindrical cap with shaggy scales that dissolves into black ink from the bottom up. Edible only when young and white.

common-inkcap.name: Common inkcap
common-inkcap.habitat: Clustered on buried wood, stumps, gardens, grass
common-inkcap.summary: Grey, smooth, bell-shaped caps in clusters that dissolve into ink. Becomes toxic if you drink alcohol up to three days before or after eating it.

birch-polypore.name: Birch polypore
birch-polypore.habitat: Only on birch, usually dead or dying trees
birch-polypore.summary: Smooth, white to pale brown kidney-shaped bracket on birch. Not a food, but an antiseptic dressing, tinder, and a strop for honing knives.

tinder-fungus.name: Tinder fungus (horse's hoof)
tinder-fungus.habitat: On birch (especially in Scotland and northern England) and beech (in the south)
tinder-fungus.summary: Grey, hoof-shaped, very hard bracket on birch and beech. Its inner layer (amadou) catches a spark from flint and steel and smoulders for a long time.

cramp-balls.name: Cramp balls (King Alfred's cakes)
cramp-balls.habitat: Dead or dying ash trees and fallen ash branches, sometimes beech
cramp-balls.summary: Hard, black, round lumps on dead ash with concentric rings inside. A dry one catches a spark and smoulders: an excellent natural ember extender.

sulphur-tuft.name: Sulphur tuft
sulphur-tuft.habitat: Dense clusters on rotting stumps and logs of broadleaf and conifer trees; very common
sulphur-tuft.summary: Dense clusters of sulphur-yellow caps with greenish gills on dead wood. Very bitter and poisonous; often confused with honey fungus.

honey-fungus.name: Honey fungus
honey-fungus.habitat: Dense clusters at the bases of living and dead trees and stumps, and on buried roots; very common
honey-fungus.summary: Clusters of honey-brown caps with dark central scales, white gills and a ring, on wood. Edible only if well cooked, and many people react. Not for beginners.

st-georges-mushroom.name: St George's mushroom
st-georges-mushroom.season: Apr–Jun (traditionally from St George's Day, 23 April)
st-georges-mushroom.habitat: Grassland, road verges, woodland edges and hedgerows, often in rings; especially on chalk and limestone
st-georges-mushroom.summary: Chunky cream-white spring mushroom with crowded white gills and a strong mealy smell of flour or cucumber. Deadly white lookalikes exist.

deadly-fibrecap.name: Deadly fibrecap
deadly-fibrecap.habitat: Under beech and lime on chalk and limestone, parks and woodland edges
deadly-fibrecap.summary: Cream-white mushroom with a conical, radially fibrous, splitting cap that bruises brick-red. Contains high levels of muscarine; has killed in the UK.

fools-funnel.name: Fool's funnel
fools-funnel.habitat: Lawns, pasture, parks, often in rings and among fairy ring champignons
fools-funnel.summary: Small, chalky-white, slightly funnel-shaped grassland mushroom with gills running down the stem. Rich in muscarine.

fairy-ring-champignon.name: Fairy ring champignon
fairy-ring-champignon.habitat: Lawns, pasture, golf courses, in rings of dark green grass
fairy-ring-champignon.summary: Small buff mushroom with widely spaced gills and a tough, bendy stem, growing in rings in short grass. Edible, but it grows alongside the deadly fool's funnel.

hedgehog-fungus.name: Hedgehog fungus
hedgehog-fungus.habitat: Broadleaf and conifer woods, often in rings or troops
hedgehog-fungus.summary: Cream to pale orange cap with soft spines underneath instead of gills. One of the safest edible wild fungi in the UK.

parasol.name: Parasol
parasol.habitat: Grassy clearings, woodland edges, pasture, dunes
parasol.summary: Very tall mushroom with a broad, brown-scaled cap, a snakeskin-patterned stem and a movable double ring. Small lookalikes are deadly.

brown-rollrim.name: Brown roll-rim
brown-rollrim.habitat: Woods and heaths, especially under birch; very common
brown-rollrim.summary: Brown, funnel-like mushroom with a strongly inrolled rim and soft gills that bruise dark brown. Once eaten, now known to cause fatal immune reactions.

false-morel.name: False morel
false-morel.habitat: Conifer woods and plantations on sandy soils, especially in Scotland
false-morel.summary: Reddish-brown, brain-like convoluted cap in spring conifer woods. Contains a rocket-fuel-related toxin; never eat it.

morel.name: Morel
morel.habitat: Disturbed ground, old orchards, woodland edges (ash, elm), burnt ground, wood-chip
morel.summary: Spring mushroom with a honeycomb-pitted cap that is completely hollow from top to bottom. Must be cooked.

amethyst-deceiver.name: Amethyst deceiver
amethyst-deceiver.habitat: Broadleaf and conifer woods, very common in leaf litter
amethyst-deceiver.summary: Small, entirely violet-purple mushroom with widely spaced gills, fading pale when dry (hence "deceiver"). Edible, but lilac lookalikes are toxic.

wood-blewit.name: Wood blewit
wood-blewit.habitat: Woodland leaf litter, hedgerows, compost heaps, gardens
wood-blewit.summary: Lilac-blue gilled mushroom with a perfumed smell, appearing late in the year. Must be cooked; easily confused with poisonous webcaps.

turkey-tail.name: Turkey tail
turkey-tail.habitat: Dead broadleaf wood, stumps and logs; very common
turkey-tail.summary: Thin, leathery, fan-shaped brackets with velvety concentric bands of brown, grey and blue. Too tough to eat; used for medicinal tea.

dryads-saddle.name: Dryad's saddle
dryads-saddle.habitat: Living and dead broadleaf trees, especially sycamore, elm and beech
dryads-saddle.summary: Large cream bracket patterned with brown feather-like scales, with a smell of watermelon rind. Edible only when young and soft.

beefsteak-fungus.name: Beefsteak fungus
beefsteak-fungus.habitat: Living oak and sweet chestnut, often low on the trunk
beefsteak-fungus.summary: Liver-red, tongue-like bracket on oak that "bleeds" red juice and has sour, meat-like streaked flesh.

scarlet-elf-cup.name: Scarlet elf cup
scarlet-elf-cup.habitat: Fallen, mossy, rotting branches in damp woods and hedges
scarlet-elf-cup.summary: Brilliant scarlet cups on mossy sticks in late winter: easy to recognise and a sign of clean, damp air.

saffron-milkcap.name: Saffron milkcap
saffron-milkcap.habitat: On the ground under pines, especially Scots pine, often in grass or moss at plantation edges; widespread but commonest in Scotland and on sandy soils
saffron-milkcap.summary: Carrot-orange cap with darker concentric rings, orange gills and orange milk that oozes when you cut it. Bruises and ages green. Lookalikes with white milk are poisonous.

woolly-milkcap.name: Woolly milkcap
woolly-milkcap.habitat: Always with birch: heaths, birch scrub, woodland edges, parks and gardens with birch trees
woolly-milkcap.summary: Pale salmon-pink cap with darker rings and a shaggy, woolly beard around the inrolled edge. White, fiercely hot milk. Causes violent vomiting and diarrhoea.

ugly-milkcap.name: Ugly milkcap
ugly-milkcap.habitat: Under birch in woods, heaths and parks, sometimes with spruce; often half-hidden in moss and leaf litter; common
ugly-milkcap.summary: Dull olive-brown to almost black, sticky cap, cream gills that stain brown, and white, burning-hot milk. Contains a toxin that damaged DNA in laboratory tests.

charcoal-burner.name: Charcoal burner
charcoal-burner.habitat: Broadleaf woods, especially under beech and oak, sometimes birch; very common across the UK
charcoal-burner.summary: A brittlegill with a cap blending purple, slate-blue, grey and green, and white gills that feel greasy and bend rather than crumble. Green forms must be told from the death cap.

the-sickener.name: The sickener
the-sickener.habitat: Damp conifer woods, especially under pine, often in moss or sphagnum bogs; common
the-sickener.summary: Shiny cherry-red cap, pure white gills and a pure white, brittle stem. Tastes burningly hot. Causes vomiting and diarrhoea, as the name says.

orange-birch-bolete.name: Orange birch bolete
orange-birch-bolete.habitat: Always with birch: birch woods, heaths and moorland edges with heather; common, especially in the north and west
orange-birch-bolete.summary: Big orange cap, grey pores and a tall white stem covered in black scales. The flesh turns grey-violet then blackish when cut. Must be thoroughly cooked.

brown-birch-bolete.name: Brown birch bolete
brown-birch-bolete.habitat: Only under birch, in woods, heaths, parks and gardens; very common across the UK
brown-birch-bolete.summary: Grey-brown cap, pale greyish pores and a slender white stem covered in dark scales, always with birch. Soft and spongy with age. Must be thoroughly cooked.

slippery-jack.name: Slippery jack
slippery-jack.habitat: Under pines, especially Scots pine in young plantations, heaths and on sandy soils; common
slippery-jack.summary: Chocolate-brown, very slimy cap, small yellow pores, and a ring on the stem that turns purplish-brown. The slimy skin upsets some people.

velvet-shank.name: Velvet shank
velvet-shank.habitat: Clusters on dead and dying broadleaf wood, especially elm, ash, beech, oak and willow, also gorse; stumps, fallen logs and trunks
velvet-shank.summary: Clusters of sticky orange-brown caps on dead wood in winter, with a velvety, dark brown to black stem and a white spore print. The deadly funeral bell grows in the same places.

horn-of-plenty.name: Horn of plenty
horn-of-plenty.habitat: In leaf litter under beech and oak, often on clay or chalky soils and along banks and ditches; local, but often in large groups
horn-of-plenty.summary: Thin, hollow, black-grey trumpets with no gills: smooth or faintly wrinkled grey outside, sooty black inside. Very hard to spot in leaf litter.

trumpet-chanterelle.name: Trumpet chanterelle
trumpet-chanterelle.habitat: Mossy conifer and mixed woods on acid soils, often among moss or on very rotten wood; commonest in Scotland, Wales and the west
trumpet-chanterelle.summary: Small brown funnel caps with grey, blunt, forked ridges underneath and a hollow yellow stem. Grows in the same mossy conifer woods as the deadly webcap.

cauliflower-fungus.name: Cauliflower fungus
cauliflower-fungus.habitat: At the base of conifers, especially Scots pine and other pines, or beside pine stumps; often returns to the same tree each year
cauliflower-fungus.summary: A cream to pale tan ball of flat, wavy, curly lobes like a brain, a sponge or a pile of egg noodles, at the foot of pines. No gills or pores.

hen-of-the-woods.name: Hen of the woods
hen-of-the-woods.habitat: At the base of old oaks, sometimes beech or sweet chestnut, on roots and stumps; occasional, mainly in southern England
hen-of-the-woods.summary: A clump of many small grey-brown, fan-shaped caps on branching white stalks, with white pores underneath, at the base of oaks. Flesh does not blacken.

giant-polypore.name: Giant polypore
giant-polypore.habitat: At the base of beech, sometimes oak and other broadleaves, or around stumps, growing from roots; common in parks and woods
giant-polypore.summary: Huge rosettes of thick, brown, fan-shaped caps at the base of beech trees. Pores and flesh bruise black. A sign of root rot: the tree may fall.

shaggy-parasol.name: Shaggy parasol
shaggy-parasol.habitat: Woodland (especially conifer litter), hedgerows, gardens, compost heaps and rich, disturbed ground
shaggy-parasol.summary: Medium to large mushroom with coarse, upturned brown scales on a whitish cap, a smooth stem with a movable ring, and flesh that turns orange-red when cut. Upsets many people.

stinking-dapperling.name: Stinking dapperling
stinking-dapperling.habitat: Leaf litter in woods, path edges, gardens, lawns, nettle beds and compost; rich, disturbed soil; common
stinking-dapperling.summary: A small parasol-like mushroom (2–5 cm) with rings of reddish-brown scales on a white cap and a rubbery, gassy smell. Its small relatives include deadly species.

livid-pinkgill.name: Livid pinkgill
livid-pinkgill.habitat: Broadleaf woods on clay or chalky soils, under oak, beech and hornbeam; parks; often in rings; local, mainly in the south
livid-pinkgill.summary: A large, fleshy, grey-white mushroom with gills that are yellowish when young and salmon-pink when old, a pink spore print and a mealy smell. Causes severe vomiting and diarrhoea.

the-miller.name: The miller
the-miller.habitat: Grassy clearings, rides and woodland edges near broadleaf trees and conifers; often near ceps
the-miller.summary: Small white to pale grey mushroom with a soft, suede-like cap, gills running down the stem that turn pink, and a strong smell of fresh bread dough. Deadly white lookalikes grow in the same grass.

trooping-funnel.name: Trooping funnel
trooping-funnel.habitat: In troops and large rings in open broadleaf woods, clearings, rides and under hedges, often on chalk and limestone
trooping-funnel.summary: Tall, pale buff funnel mushroom with a central hump in the middle of the funnel, deep-running cream gills and a stout stem. Grows in big rings in late autumn.

clouded-agaric.name: Clouded agaric
clouded-agaric.habitat: Troops and rings in leaf litter of broadleaf and conifer woods, also hedgerows and parks; very common in late autumn
clouded-agaric.summary: Large, fleshy mushroom with a cloud-grey cap, cream gills running slightly down the stem and a strong sickly-sweet smell. Once eaten, now known to upset many people.

false-death-cap.name: False death cap
false-death-cap.habitat: Broadleaf and conifer woods on acid soils, especially with beech, oak, birch and pine; very common
false-death-cap.summary: Pale lemon-yellow or white cap with flat patches of veil, a ring, and a large rimmed bulb at the base. Smells of raw potato. Not seriously poisonous, but far too close to the death cap.

tawny-grisette.name: Tawny grisette
tawny-grisette.habitat: Broadleaf and conifer woods on acid soils, especially with birch, also oak, beech and pine; very common
tawny-grisette.summary: Orange-brown cap with a grooved edge, white gills, a slender stem with no ring, and a tall white sac (volva) at the base. An Amanita: poisonous raw and never worth the risk.

magpie-inkcap.name: Magpie inkcap
magpie-inkcap.habitat: Beech woods on chalk and limestone, also other broadleaf woods; scattered, commonest in southern England
magpie-inkcap.summary: A tall, bell-shaped inkcap with a dark brown-black cap broken into white patches, like a magpie. Gills turn to black ink. Poisonous.

stinkhorn.name: Stinkhorn
stinkhorn.habitat: Woods (especially broadleaf), gardens and hedges, near rotting wood and roots; very common
stinkhorn.summary: A white, spongy, phallus-shaped stalk topped with a cap of foul-smelling olive-green slime that draws flies. Grows from a white "egg" that can be mistaken for a puffball or an Amanita egg.

adder.name: Adder
adder.season: Active Mar–Oct; basks on sunny mornings in spring
adder.habitat: Heathland, moorland, rough grassland, woodland edges, sand dunes, bracken slopes, across mainland Britain (not Ireland)
adder.summary: The UK's only venomous snake: grey-cream or brown with a bold dark zig-zag along the back. Bites are rare and rarely fatal, but always need hospital.

grass-snake.name: Grass snake
grass-snake.habitat: Near ponds, rivers, ditches, wet meadows and gardens in England and Wales
grass-snake.summary: Harmless olive-green snake with a yellow and black collar behind the head. Swims well; plays dead or releases a foul smell if handled.

slow-worm.name: Slow worm
slow-worm.habitat: Grassland, heaths, gardens, woodland edges, under logs and stones
slow-worm.summary: A legless lizard, not a snake: smooth, shiny, bronze-grey, with eyelids that blink. Completely harmless.

tick.name: Sheep tick
tick.habitat: Long grass, bracken, heather and woodland, especially where there are deer or sheep; also urban parks
tick.summary: Tiny blood-sucking arachnid that waits on vegetation and can transmit Lyme disease. Remove it promptly and correctly.

common-wasp.name: Common wasp
common-wasp.habitat: Everywhere; nests in the ground, banks, hollow trees, lofts
common-wasp.summary: Black-and-yellow social wasp that can sting repeatedly. Ground nests disturbed while gathering firewood or sitting down cause multiple stings.

hornet.name: European hornet
hornet.habitat: Woodland, parkland, hollow trees, mainly in southern England
hornet.summary: Large brown-and-yellow wasp (up to 3.5 cm). Less aggressive than common wasps away from the nest, but its sting is more painful.

false-widow.name: Noble false widow
false-widow.season: All year, more noticed in autumn
false-widow.habitat: Houses, sheds, fences, walls; mainly southern and central England, spreading
false-widow.summary: Bulbous, glossy brown spider with cream markings. Bites are uncommon and usually like a bee sting, occasionally infected.

highland-midge.name: Highland midge
highland-midge.season: May–Sep, worst Jun–Aug at dawn and dusk
highland-midge.habitat: Damp, still, shady upland areas, especially in western Scotland
highland-midge.summary: Tiny biting fly that swarms in still, damp, dull weather. Not dangerous, but miserable; pick breezy, open camps.

red-deer.name: Red deer
red-deer.habitat: Scottish Highlands and islands, Exmoor, the Lake District, the New Forest, Thetford, and parts of East Anglia and the Peak District
red-deer.summary: The UK's largest land mammal. Stags are dangerous during the autumn rut. Venison may only be taken by authorised stalkers.

roe-deer.name: Roe deer
roe-deer.habitat: Woodland and farmland across most of Britain
roe-deer.summary: Small, graceful deer with no visible tail, a white rump patch, and a dog-like bark when alarmed.

wild-boar.name: Wild boar
wild-boar.habitat: Forest of Dean (largest population); small populations in southern England and Scotland
wild-boar.summary: Bristly, dark wild pig that is shy but dangerous if surprised, cornered, or with piglets, or if a dog approaches.

badger.name: Badger
badger.habitat: Woodland edges, hedgerows and farmland across the UK
badger.summary: Black-and-white striped face, grey body, nocturnal. Heavily protected; its setts and paths are good signs of the land.

red-fox.name: Red fox
red-fox.summary: Rusty-red dog-like animal with a white-tipped bushy tail. Raids food stores; its tracks run in a neat straight line.

rabbit.name: European rabbit
rabbit.habitat: Grassland, field edges, dunes, heaths and woodland edges across the UK
rabbit.summary: Common grazing mammal living in warrens. Edible, but taking it is governed by strict law, and it is too lean to live on.

brown-hare.name: Brown hare
brown-hare.habitat: Open farmland and grassland in lowland Britain
brown-hare.summary: Larger than a rabbit, with long black-tipped ears and long hind legs. Lives in the open, not in burrows. Leave it alone.

grey-squirrel.name: Grey squirrel
grey-squirrel.habitat: Woods, parks and gardens throughout England, Wales and much of Scotland
grey-squirrel.summary: Common, invasive, North American squirrel. Edible meat, but take it only with landowner permission and by legal means.

red-squirrel.name: Red squirrel
red-squirrel.habitat: Conifer forests of Scotland, the Lake District, Northumberland, Anglesey, the Isle of Wight and Brownsea Island
red-squirrel.summary: Native squirrel, russet-red with ear tufts. Strictly protected and endangered: never harm it.

pheasant.name: Pheasant
pheasant.habitat: Farmland, woodland edges, hedgerows; heavily released on shooting estates
pheasant.summary: Large game bird; males copper with a green head and red wattles. Edible, but it belongs to the holder of the shooting rights.

wood-pigeon.name: Wood pigeon
wood-pigeon.habitat: Farmland, woods, parks and gardens everywhere
wood-pigeon.summary: The UK's commonest large pigeon: grey, with a white neck patch and white wing bars in flight. Good dark meat.

brown-trout.name: Brown trout
brown-trout.season: Open season varies by area (typically mid-March to early October in England and Wales; mid-March to early October in Scotland)
brown-trout.habitat: Clean, cool rivers, streams, lochs and lakes throughout the UK
brown-trout.summary: Native freshwater fish with dark spots and red spots ringed with pale halos. Edible; fishing requires permission and (in England and Wales) a rod licence.

signal-crayfish.name: Signal crayfish
signal-crayfish.season: All year, most active in summer
signal-crayfish.habitat: Rivers, streams, canals, lakes and gravel pits across England, Wales and parts of Scotland
signal-crayfish.summary: Large invasive American crayfish, with a white-turquoise patch at the claw hinge and red claw undersides. Edible, but trapping requires authorisation.

white-clawed-crayfish.name: White-clawed crayfish
white-clawed-crayfish.habitat: Clean, stony, limestone rivers and streams; now rare
white-clawed-crayfish.summary: The UK's only native crayfish, small, with pale undersides to its claws. Endangered and protected: never take one.

weever-fish.name: Lesser weever
weever-fish.habitat: Buried in sand in shallow water on sandy beaches, especially in southern and western Britain at low tide
weever-fish.summary: Small sandy fish that buries itself in shallow water, with venomous spines on its back. Treading on one is agony: treat with hot water.

lions-mane-jellyfish.name: Lion's mane jellyfish
lions-mane-jellyfish.habitat: Coastal waters, especially northern and western Britain
lions-mane-jellyfish.summary: Large red-brown jellyfish with masses of long trailing tentacles. Painful stings, even from dead ones on the beach.

mussel.name: Common mussel
mussel.habitat: Rocky shores, piers and estuaries, attached in beds between the tides
mussel.summary: Blue-black shellfish in beds on rocks and piers. Edible, but shellfish poisoning and sewage pollution are real risks.

periwinkle.name: Common periwinkle
periwinkle.habitat: Rocks and seaweed on the shore between the tides
periwinkle.summary: Small dark spiral sea snail on rocky shores. Boil and pick the meat out with a pin.

mackerel.name: Atlantic mackerel
mackerel.habitat: Coastal waters around the UK in summer, in shoals
mackerel.summary: Tiger-striped silver-green sea fish that arrives inshore in summer shoals and can be caught from piers and rocks with simple feathers.

cattle.name: Cattle
cattle.season: All year; most danger when cows have young calves (spring)
cattle.summary: Not wildlife, but cows with calves, and bulls, injure and kill walkers in the UK every year, especially people with dogs.

oak-processionary-moth.name: Oak processionary moth
oak-processionary-moth.season: Caterpillars Apr–Jul; old nests stay hazardous all year
oak-processionary-moth.habitat: Oak trees, mainly in London and the surrounding counties of south-east England; occasional outbreaks elsewhere
oak-processionary-moth.summary: Invasive moth whose grey, hairy caterpillars live in silk nests on oaks. Their tiny hairs cause rashes, sore eyes and throat irritation. Don't touch, camp under or burn them.

brown-tail-moth.name: Brown-tail moth
brown-tail-moth.habitat: Hedgerows and scrub, especially hawthorn, blackthorn, bramble and sea buckthorn; mainly coastal south and east England, also some towns
brown-tail-moth.summary: Dark brown, white-tufted caterpillars that live in tough silk tents on hedges. Their hairs cause an intensely itchy rash and can affect eyes and breathing.

honey-bee.name: Honey bee
honey-bee.habitat: Everywhere with flowers; hives on farms and in gardens; wild colonies in hollow trees, walls and chimneys
honey-bee.summary: Slim golden-brown bee that stings once and leaves its sting behind. One sting is painful; many stings, or an allergy, are an emergency.

cleg.name: Cleg
cleg.season: May–Sep, worst on warm, humid, thundery days
cleg.habitat: Damp woods, river banks, moorland and pasture near cattle and horses across the UK
cleg.summary: Grey, silent biting fly whose painful bite can swell badly and become infected. Larger horseflies bite the same way.

harvest-mite.name: Harvest mite
harvest-mite.habitat: Long grass, chalk downland, heaths, woodland edges, lawns and gardens, especially on dry, sunny ground
harvest-mite.summary: Almost invisible orange larvae that bite where clothing is tight, causing clusters of fiercely itchy red spots that appear hours later. Harmless but miserable.

portuguese-man-o-war.name: Portuguese man o' war
portuguese-man-o-war.season: Washed up mainly Aug–Nov after strong westerly winds
portuguese-man-o-war.habitat: Open Atlantic; stranded on beaches in south-west England, Wales, Ireland and western Scotland
portuguese-man-o-war.summary: A blue-purple gas float with long, extremely painful stinging tentacles. Stings are severe; dead ones on the beach still sting. Don't touch.

compass-jellyfish.name: Compass jellyfish
compass-jellyfish.habitat: Coastal waters and beaches, mainly southern and western Britain
compass-jellyfish.summary: Whitish jellyfish with brown V-shaped markings radiating like a compass. Its long tentacles give a painful sting, even when stranded.

moon-jellyfish.name: Moon jellyfish
moon-jellyfish.season: Apr–Sep, often in large swarms in summer
moon-jellyfish.habitat: All UK coasts; often stranded in large numbers on beaches
moon-jellyfish.summary: The commonest UK jellyfish: a clear saucer with four purple rings. Its sting is very weak and most people feel nothing.

common-toad.name: Common toad
common-toad.season: Active Feb–Oct; migrates to breeding ponds Feb–Apr, often across roads at night
common-toad.habitat: Woods, gardens, fields and heaths across Great Britain (not Ireland); breeds in larger, deeper ponds and lakes
common-toad.summary: Warty brown amphibian that crawls rather than hops. Its skin glands make a poison: never eat a toad or its spawn, and wash your hands after handling.

great-crested-newt.name: Great crested newt
great-crested-newt.season: In ponds Feb–Jul; on land under logs and stones the rest of the year
great-crested-newt.habitat: Ponds without fish in lowland England, Wales and southern Scotland; nearby grassland, scrub, hedges and woodland
great-crested-newt.summary: The UK's largest newt: dark, warty, with a bright orange, black-blotched belly. Strictly protected: even disturbing it is an offence.

smooth-snake.name: Smooth snake
smooth-snake.habitat: Dry lowland heath with heather and gorse on sandy soil: Dorset, Hampshire (New Forest) and Surrey, with small reintroduced populations elsewhere in southern England
smooth-snake.summary: Rare, harmless grey-brown snake with rows of small dark spots and a dark eye-stripe. Often mistaken for an adder. Strictly protected.

hedgehog.name: Hedgehog
hedgehog.habitat: Gardens, hedgerows, woodland edges, parks and farmland across the UK
hedgehog.summary: Spiny, nocturnal insect-eater that hibernates in leaf piles and brushwood. Check heaps before you burn them. Protected from trapping and cruelty; not a food.

otter.name: Eurasian otter
otter.season: All year; mostly at night, but by day on Scottish coasts
otter.habitat: Rivers, lakes, lochs, marshes and rocky coasts across the UK, especially Scotland, Wales and western England
otter.summary: Large, sleek, brown aquatic mammal with a thick tapering tail. Its fishy-smelling droppings on rocks show clean water and fish. Fully protected.

american-mink.name: American mink
american-mink.habitat: Rivers, canals, lakes, marshes and coasts across most of the UK
american-mink.summary: Small, near-black, ferret-like predator escaped from fur farms. It kills water voles, seabirds and poultry, and bites hard if cornered.

grey-seal.name: Grey seal
grey-seal.season: All year; pups born Aug–Jan (earlier in the south-west, later on the east coast)
grey-seal.habitat: Rocky coasts, islands, sandbanks and beaches all round the UK, especially Scotland, Wales, Cornwall, Norfolk and Lincolnshire
grey-seal.summary: Large seal with a long "Roman" nose. Can bite hard if approached, and bites infect easily. Leave pups alone: they are rarely abandoned.

herring-gull.name: Herring gull
herring-gull.season: All year; aggressive near nests and chicks Apr–Aug
herring-gull.habitat: Coasts, harbours, seaside towns, rubbish tips, fields and roofs across the UK
herring-gull.summary: Big grey-and-white gull that snatches food and dive-bombs people near its chicks in summer. A declining, protected bird: never harm it or take its eggs.

great-skua.name: Great skua
great-skua.season: On breeding grounds Apr–Sep; dive-bombs mostly Jun–Aug
great-skua.habitat: Coastal moorland in Shetland, Orkney, the Outer Hebrides and the far north of Scotland
great-skua.summary: Big, dark brown seabird that dive-bombs walkers who come near its nest, striking the head with its feet. Hold something above your head and walk away.

mute-swan.name: Mute swan
mute-swan.season: All year; aggressive when nesting and with cygnets Mar–Aug
mute-swan.habitat: Rivers, canals, lakes, reservoirs, estuaries and sheltered coasts across the UK
mute-swan.summary: Large white swan with an orange bill and black knob. Males defending nests or cygnets charge people, dogs and paddlers. Protected: never harm or eat one.

brown-crab.name: Brown crab
brown-crab.season: All year; best Apr–Nov; inshore in rock pools mainly in summer
brown-crab.habitat: Rocky shores, under boulders and weed at low tide, and offshore on rough ground all round the UK
brown-crab.summary: Heavy reddish-brown crab with a "pie-crust" edge and black-tipped claws. Good food, but minimum sizes apply, it must be cooked fresh, and the claws can crush fingers.

common-limpet.name: Common limpet
common-limpet.habitat: Clamped to rocks on rocky shores all round the UK, from high to low tide
common-limpet.summary: Cone-shaped shell clamped to rocks. Tough but filling survival food, easy to collect. Cook thoroughly and gather only from clean shores.

cockle.name: Common cockle
cockle.season: All year, but regulated beds often open only in set seasons
cockle.habitat: Just under the surface of sand and muddy sand on the lower shore, especially estuaries and bays such as the Burry Inlet, Morecambe Bay, the Wash and the Thames estuary
cockle.summary: Ribbed, rounded shellfish dug from sandy shores. Good food when cooked thoroughly, but beds are often regulated or closed, and tidal flats can trap and drown you.

pollack.name: Pollack
pollack.habitat: Rocky coasts, kelp beds, harbour walls, piers and wrecks, especially in western and northern Britain
pollack.summary: Bronze-green sea fish with a strongly curved lateral line and a jutting lower jaw, caught from rocks and piers. Good white fish, but current bag limits may apply.

pike.name: Pike
pike.season: Rivers in England and Wales closed 15 Mar–15 Jun; lakes and canals depend on local rules
pike.habitat: Slow rivers, lakes, lochs, canals, drains and gravel pits with weed beds across the UK
pike.summary: Long green predatory fish with a duck-bill snout and a mouth full of sharp teeth. Edible but bony; handle with care, and take one only where the rules allow.

european-eel.name: European eel
european-eel.season: All year; young eels (elvers) run upriver Feb–Jun
european-eel.habitat: Rivers, streams, ditches, lakes, ponds, estuaries and coasts all over the UK
european-eel.summary: Snake-like fish that is now critically endangered. Rod anglers must return every eel they catch in England and Wales, and eel fishing in Scotland needs authorisation. Don't keep one.

liberty-cap.name: Liberty cap
liberty-cap.habitat: Grazed or fertilised grassland, especially wet sheep and cattle pasture, also lawns and playing fields; in grass, never on wood or directly on dung
liberty-cap.summary: Small, slender grassland mushroom with a pointed, nipple-topped brown cap. A Class A drug under UK law, and it grows among deadly little brown mushrooms.

wavy-cap.name: Wavy cap
